entries.summary: If you haven’t chosen how to bill Copilot code review for members with a Copilot license, those reviews will be billed to your organization starting December 30, 2026.
entries.text: If you haven’t chosen how to bill Copilot code review for members with a Copilot license, those reviews will be billed to your organization starting December 30, 2026. To keep billing unchanged, select Member before then. This change applies to organizations and enterprises with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise. What’s changing Today, when no billing choice is saved, reviews by members who have a paid Copilot license use the member’s Copilot entitlement. Starting December 30, 2026, those reviews will be billed to the organization that owns the repository. Accounts that don’t have AI Credits paid usage enabled, have a billing lock, or have no billable customer will be set to Member instead. If you already chose Member or Organization, your choice stays in effect. The separate setting for members without a Copilot license doesn’t change. Keep member billing Until then, unset settings show Default (Member) with a notice about the change. To keep using members’ Copilot entitlements, select Member in your enterprise or organization Copilot policy settings. That choice stays in effect after the default changes. If your enterprise manages this setting, an enterprise owner makes this choice. Organization billing requires AI Credits paid usage and can increase your organization’s spending. To learn more, see Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot. The post Copilot code review billing will default to the organization appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Copilot code review billing will default to the organization

entries.text: Starting December 1, 2026, we’re migrating notifications on GitHub.com over the course of a week to make subscriptions more predictable, correct unexpected behavior, and support the growing scale of activity. During the rollout, notifications may behave differently for different users. No action is required, but the changes below may affect how you manage and filter notifications. This does not apply to GitHub Enterprise Server. What is changing Routine activity won’t resubscribe you: Previously, after manually unsubscribing, notification activities such as commenting, submitting a pull request review, changing a thread’s state, or merge queue activity resulted in a re-subscription. Now, those actions leave you unsubscribed. Being mentioned, assigned, or receiving a pull request review request will continue to resubscribe you since those actions ask for your attention. Team-mention notifications will reflect current team membership and mentions: Previously, you could continue receiving notifications after a team mention was removed or you left the team. If you joined a team after it was mentioned, you wouldn’t receive notifications for future activity. Now, removing the mention or leaving the team stops future notifications based on that team mention, so you may receive fewer notifications. entries.summary: Open or closed doesn’t always tell you where an issue stands.
entries.text: Open or closed doesn’t always tell you where an issue stands. You can now use more specific statuses to give your team and agents shared context about what’s in flight and what to work on next, then visualize your progress with repository boards. Issue statuses Track progress directly on an issue. Choose a status when creating an issue or change it from the issue header. You’ll see it reflected in issue icons across the repository issues page, the issues dashboard, and repository boards, where you can use the status: filter to find the issues you’re looking for. Available statuses are: Backlog Todo In progress In review Done Not planned Duplicate Automated status updates. To help keep your statuses accurate, the following automations are applied to your issues: Linking a draft pull request to an issue moves the issue to In progress. Marking a draft pull request as Ready for review moves the issue to In review. Linking an open pull request to an issue moves the issue to In review. Assigning a user to an issue moves it to Todo. Assigning an agent to an issue moves it to In progress. If a GitHub Project has a status value that matches an issue status, changing either status updates the other. GraphQL, REST API, and MCP server support. Automations and agents can read an issue’s status, set a status, and choose an initial status when creating an issue. entries.summary: The GitHub Code Quality upload-code-coverage action now checks that your coverage report is in Cobertura XML format.
entries.text: The GitHub Code Quality upload-code-coverage action now checks that your coverage report is in Cobertura XML format. If it isn’t in a supported format, the upload step fails and the Actions log shows this error: This file is not a Cobertura XML report. Upload a Cobertura XML report. Previously, these uploads appeared to succeed, but no coverage showed up on your pull requests. Now you’ll find out about the problem in the workflow run, with a clear next step. If your workflow begins failing with this error, configure your test framework to output Cobertura XML, or convert your report to Cobertura XML before the upload step. We’ve also made processing more forgiving for valid Cobertura reports. We no longer reject a report because of minor structural issues, and we skip individual lines that don’t have a usable line number or hit count instead of discarding the whole report. To use code coverage, you need GitHub Code Quality enabled for your repository. This change is available now on GitHub Enterprise Cloud and GitHub Team, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. It isn’t available on GitHub Enterprise Server. Learn more about setting up code coverage for your repository on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. The post Code coverage uploads now flag invalid report formats appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Code coverage uploads now flag invalid report formats

entries.summary: Starting December 1, 2026, usage reports that include a username column will also include a user_id column next to it.
entries.text: Starting December 1, 2026, usage reports that include a username column will also include a user_id column next to it. Every column after username will move one position to the right. This change applies to the detailed usage report, the AI usage report, and the premium request usage report, including exports you create with the GitHub REST API. The summarized usage report won’t change. These changes apply to all GitHub Enterprise Cloud account types and standalone organizations on GitHub Team. What you need to do If your scripts or tools read these reports by column position, update them to read columns by header name before December 1. What’s changing The user_id column contains the ID of the account that generated the usage, including bot accounts. It’s empty for usage that isn’t tied to an account. With this column, you can: Identify usage from deleted accounts, which currently have an empty username. Follow a user’s usage after they change their username. Match report rows to events in your audit log. Usage from different deleted accounts will also appear on separate rows instead of combined in one row with an empty username. We’ll calculate amounts the same way, but because we round each row separately, totals you add up from the report may differ slightly in the last decimal places. To learn more, see Usage report fields. The post Usage reports will include a user ID column starting December 1 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Usage reports will include a user ID column starting December 1

entries.summary: Organization owners can now let people work on repository security advisories, including private vulnerability reports, through custom repository roles.
entries.text: Organization owners can now let people work on repository security advisories, including private vulnerability reports, through custom repository roles. You no longer have to make them repository administrators or give them the organization-wide security manager role. Four new permissions are available under Security when you create or edit a custom repository role: View security advisories: view draft security advisories, their status, and comments. Create, Edit, and Manage security advisories: everything in View, plus Create and Edit advisories, comment, manage collaborators, and create a temporary private fork. Accept private vulnerability reports and close or reopen security advisories: requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage. Publish security advisories and request CVEs: requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage. Assign the role to users and teams on only the repositories where they need it. The permissions apply to both repository security advisories and private vulnerability reports, so you can give a team access to the repositories they maintain without exposing advisories across your whole organization. A few things to know: Merging changes from a temporary private fork still requires a repository administrator or security manager. People with any of these new permissions can’t delete a temporary private fork. entries.title: Security advisory permissions are now generally available

entries.summary: GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.23 is now available and introduces new capabilities across the platform.
entries.text: GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.23 is now available and introduces new capabilities across the platform. Here are a few highlights in the 3.23 release: When working in GitHub Projects, you can create more precise project views by combining filters with logical OR, explicit AND, and parentheses for grouping. For example, (status:Done OR status:Todo) is:issue shows issues with either status. If your enterprise uses GitHub Secret Protection, you can detect unstructured secrets entirely within your network using AI secret detection on GHES, including in air-gapped environments. A self-contained, fine-tuned model runs on the appliance’s CPU without a GPU, hosted LLM, or outbound connection. This feature is in public preview and subject to change. As a developer, you can identify known malicious packages in PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, Rust, and Composer through the GitHub Advisory Database, in addition to npm. The database automatically ingests malware advisories from OpenSSF’s malicious-packages repository to expand coverage across these ecosystems. By default, Dependabot waits until a package version has been available on its registry for at least three days before opening a version update pull request. This cooldown gives maintainers and the community more time to detect and report compromised or buggy releases before users merge updates. entries.summary: Editor’s note (November 23, 2026): We have temporarily rolled back this change while we improve the experience based on user feedback.
entries.text: Editor’s note (November 23, 2026): We have temporarily rolled back this change while we improve the experience based on user feedback. Choose which repositories appear on the Dashboard with the new Favorite repositories section. If the new dashboard experience isn’t enabled, Top repositories remains unchanged. Select Edit or Add repositories to open the picker. Search for repositories and select or deselect them. Your selections stay visible as you search. Select Save to apply your changes. New favorites are added to the end of your list. To discard your changes, select Cancel. Your favorites sync with your pinned repositories in GitHub Mobile. Changes you make in either place appear in the other after you refresh. You can pin up to 25 repositories across both experiences. If saving would put you over the limit, you’ll see an error and your list won’t change. Leave your feedback in the GitHub Community discussion. The post Pin your favorite repositories to your dashboard appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Pin your favorite repositories to your dashboard

entries.summary: GitHub Desktop now lets you sign in with more than one account on the same host, including GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GHE.com.
entries.text: GitHub Desktop now lets you sign in with more than one account on the same host, including GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GHE.com. This has been one of the most requested features in the Desktop community. With this release, you can: Add more than one account for a single host, with no fixed limit. Associate each repository with a specific account, so clone, publish, and Git operations use the right credentials automatically. Choose an account when adding or cloning a repository that multiple signed-in accounts can access, or let Desktop infer it when only one can. Change a repository’s account association at any time from repository settings or the repository list’s context menu. Existing repositories are migrated automatically to the account you were already using, so if you only have one account per host, nothing changes for you. To get started, download the latest (GitHub Desktop 3.7.0) and open Settings/Options > Accounts to add another account, then use the new account picker when cloning, publishing, or reviewing a repository’s settings. Learn more in GitHub Desktop’s authentication documentation. The post GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host
